notes.title: Source Analysis — US v. Google Remedies Opinion (Doc. 1436, Sept 2 2025)
notes.summary: Judge Mehta's Sept 2 2025 remedies opinion permits Google to keep paying Apple for default placement (no payment ban, no price cap) while barring exclusivity and capping all distribution contracts (browsers, OEMs, carriers) at one-year annual re-election terms across a six-year (5+1) judgment effective 60 days after entry. Both parties' economists agree non-exclusive annual bidding likely compresses price even though the court doubts material query-volume will shift (rejecting plaintiffs' 31% share-shift estimate as too speculative); the opinion itself frames GenAI competition, not the decree, as the real threat to Google's position, evidenced by Apple's own testimony that Safari search volume already declined for the first time in 22 years. TAC should be modeled as a repriceable annuity under a court-imposed downward-biased repricing mechanism, not a binary event — the biggest binary tail (payment ban/divestiture) has already resolved favorably for continued payments for the life of the judgment.
notes.body:
# Source Analysis — United States v. Google LLC, D.D.C. Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM, Doc. 1436 (Remedies Memorandum Opinion, Sept. 2, 2025)

**Original source:** [[united-states-district-court]]
**Source type:** court record (memorandum opinion, ~230 printed pages)
**Source word count:** 74,310
**Your judgment:** This is the single load-bearing primary document for research question 2. It is the actual remedies ruling — not commentary about it — and it directly answers what a court can compel, on what timetable, and what the arrangement is worth under the remedy the court actually chose (as opposed to hypothetical remedies). It supersedes any secondary reporting on "what Mehta ordered."

*Suggested by [[united-states-district-court]] — source analyst's digest of the full source body*

## Thesis / Central claim

Having found Google liable for illegal monopoly maintenance in general search and general search text ads (Aug. 2024 liability opinion, a separate document), Judge Mehta orders a remedy package built on three pillars: (1) ban all *exclusive* distribution contracts for Search, Chrome, Assistant and Gemini and cap contract "stickiness" via mandatory annual re-election of default rather than multi-year lock-in; (2) require Google to share search-index and user-side data and offer search/ads syndication to "Qualified Competitors" for a period (generally five years within the six-year judgment) to erode Google's scale advantage; (3) explicitly decline the two most aggressive remedies plaintiffs sought — a full payment ban and Chrome/Android divestiture — because the court found both would cause **more** harm to consumers and distributors than they would fix, at least "for now." The judgment runs six years, effective 60 days after entry (Sept. 2 2025 + 60 days ≈ Nov. 2025), except Technical Committee provisions, effective immediately.

## Methodology / Basis of claims

This is not an empirical study; it is a judicial opinion applying Sherman Act §2 remedy doctrine (Microsoft III's "fit the wrong," causal-connection, and non-punitive-but-market-restoring standards) to an evidentiary record built during a three-week 2025 remedies trial (~50 witnesses, hundreds of exhibits) plus the carried-forward Aug. 2024 liability findings. Load-bearing evidentiary inputs the court weighs: (a) live/deposition testimony from Apple SVP Eddy Cue, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google's Android chief Sameer Samat, economists Dr. Tasneem Chipty (plaintiffs) and Dr. Kevin Murphy (Google), and executives from Mozilla, Motorola, Samsung, T-Mobile, Verizon, Perplexity, OpenAI-adjacent witnesses; (b) the "Allcott Study," an academic economic model of a Bing-default counterfactual; (c) the court's own prior liability findings (747 F. Supp. 3d 1) which it treats as established fact, not re-litigated. The court repeatedly signals it is exercising equitable discretion under uncertainty ("gaze into a crystal ball… [n]ot exactly a judge's forte," p.2) and explicitly declines to require "mathematical precision" in causal attribution (p.98).

## Key findings / Claims (with specific numbers where present)

1. **Payment ban rejected — payments for default placement are explicitly permitted, with no price or magnitude condition attached.** "So, for now, Google will be permitted to pay distributors for default placement." (p.128, RCOL III.A). This is unconditional as to amount — the court does not cap payment size, only contract structure (no exclusivity, annual reset). VERIFIED against the fetcher's headline claim.

2. **The court's central reasoning for rejecting the ban has two independent legs, both explicit:** (a) harm to distributors/consumers — "[c]utting off payments from Google almost certainly will impose substantial—in some cases, crippling—downstream harms to distribution partners, related markets, and consumers" (top-line summary, p.4); a payment ban would hand Google a "Hobson's choice" outcome where, on "day one," distributors keep Google anyway (best product) but stop getting paid — "Google thus would continue to receive a disproportionate volume of search queries for a fraction of the cost. Freed of having to pay billions in revenue share, Google's profits would increase. **Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars**" (p.121-122, citing 2022 Apple revenue share estimate of **~$20 billion**, Google 747 F. Supp. 3d at 90 ¶299 — note: explicitly a *worldwide* figure, and the court flags that Apple's U.S.-only figure would be lower but still "billions"). (b) consumer-welfare risk — both parties' economists agreed a ban would likely produce *lower* payments to distributors in the near term even in the scenario where rivals win share, because "with Google sidelined from competition, rivals would pay less than Google did to secure default or preferential placement" (p.122-123) — this is a critical, symmetric finding: the court's own logic implies degraded distributor payments under *any* scenario that removes Google's willingness to overpay for defaults, whether via ban or (implicitly) via loss of exclusivity leverage.

3. **The court explicitly rejects plaintiffs' expert's 31% share-shift estimate as "too speculative."** Full quote, footnote 11 (p.120): "Although not essential to its conclusion, the court did not find Dr. Chipty's share-shifting exercise to be persuasive. The potential 31% market shift of queries to competitors struck the court as too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior." The court notes Chipty's own assumptions shifted under cross ("she later acknowledged that such a switch might not occur on 'day one'"). VERIFIED. This finding is directly relevant to durability: if the court doubts defaults will actually move much traffic even under aggressive remedies, this cuts against a large probability-weighted downside to Apple's TAC from *demand-side* erosion (users abandoning Google) — but it says nothing about *price* erosion (Google paying less because it no longer needs exclusivity to keep the default).

4. **2021 industry-wide TAC figure confirmed: "In 2021, Google paid more than $26 billion in 'traffic acquisition costs' to distribution partners."** (p.119, citing Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d at 88-89 ¶289). The court itself adds: "That number has likely grown since." VERIFIED, exact figure and date.

5. **Exclusivity ban — confirmed for Search, Chrome, Assistant, and Gemini, with an enumerated four-part injunction.** Top-line text (p.3-4): Google "shall not enter or maintain any agreement that (1) conditions the licensing of the Play Store or any other Google application on the distribution, preloading, or placement of Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app anywhere on a device; (2) conditions the receipt of revenue share payments for the placement of one Google application… on the placement of another such application; (3) conditions the receipt of revenue share payments on maintaining Google Search, Chrome, Google Assistant, or the Gemini app on any device, browser, or search access point for **more than one year**; or (4) prohibits any partner from simultaneously distributing any other GSE, browser, or GenAI product." VERIFIED.

6. **Annual re-election / one-year term confirmed and extended by the court beyond what either party proposed for browser deals.** Google's own proposal allowed Browser Developers (i.e., Apple) to "annually set a different GSE at various search access points across different devices" as a condition of receiving revenue share (p.109-110, Google's RPFJ §III.K-L) — the court adopted this AND extended the same one-year condition to OEM/carrier agreements, which Google's draft had NOT included: "the court will impose the same one-year option as a condition of payments to OEMs and wireless carriers" (p.110-111). The court's stated rationale: "[r]ivals cannot presently access [default] channels of distribution without convincing Google's partners to break existing agreements, all of which are binding for a term of years" — i.e., contract *duration* itself (not just exclusivity) was found anticompetitive. VERIFIED — this is the annual-rebidding architecture the fetcher flagged.

7. **Six-year term confirmed, but decomposed explicitly by the court as "five years, plus an additional one year" for stand-up/administrative purposes** — not a single undifferentiated six-year clock. "[T]he court believes that a five-year term, plus an additional one year to put the infrastructure and processes in place to implement the remedies, is appropriate." (p.220). Effective date: "the final judgment shall take effect 60 days after it is entered, except as to those portions of Section X.A of the Plaintiffs' RPFJ that require the parties to take steps toward forming the Technical Committee… which will be effective immediately." (p.220). VERIFIED. Google had sought 3 years/120-day delay; plaintiffs sought 10 years/30-day delay. The court explicitly invoked the Microsoft consent decree's five-year term and its own rationale ("pace of technological change") as precedent, and separately said a 10-year term "runs the risk of growing stale" given GenAI's pace (p.220-221) — i.e., the court's own stated reason for a *shorter-than-plaintiffs-wanted* term is that AI competition, not the decree itself, is what the court is betting on to discipline Google.

8. **Apple-specific GenAI modification confirmed, narrowly targeted at Safari and Apple devices.** "[T]o leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device." (p.115). This closes a gap in Google's own draft, which defined "Third Party Generative AI Assistive Service" too narrowly (limited to "stand-alone mobile" chatbots) to clearly cover a possible future exclusive Gemini-Safari tie-up. VERIFIED.

9. **Chrome divestiture and contingent Android divestiture both rejected outright** — no five-year trigger review, no revisit mechanism specific to structural relief (contrast with the explicit "prepared to revisit a payment ban" language, finding #14 below). Reasoning: causal-connection standard for structural remedies not met (Google's dominance not shown to be primarily attributable to the illegal conduct vs. lawful factors — quality, R&D, brand); Chrome is not geographically confined to the U.S. (>80% of MAUs outside U.S.); technical/operational entanglement with Google's back-end infrastructure makes a clean sale implausible without "substantial product degradation." Plaintiffs' own expert (Chipty) estimated only a **7% share shift** from Chrome divestiture even if fully executed (p.112-113) — modest relative to the rejected 31% payment-ban estimate.

10. **Choice screens rejected, with an unusually candid admission that a remedy fashioned around device-level "choice" is pointless absent product-quality parity.** Apple's Cue, called by Google, testified: "[Apple] would 'do a choice screen, but it's not going to matter. It's not going to matter until one of the choices is actually really valuable that provides new capabilities.'" (p.191, Rem. Tr. 3849:4-7). Corroborated by the "Allcott Study" academic model: European choice screens moved Google's desktop share by only 1.3 percentage points and consumer surplus by "$0.07" — "Choice screens increase consumer surplus, but they barely move the needle in terms of market shares." (p.191).

11. **Google's own "prophylactic" contract changes are already in effect and treated by the court as a fact on the ground, not a promise.** Google updated its RSAs pre-trial to remove exclusivity-adjacent provisions and sent "eve-of-trial" waiver letters to three Android partners loosening restrictions on preloading rival "Alternative Assistive Products" (p.106-107, FOF ¶¶94-103). The court treats this as evidence the market has *already* partially moved before the final judgment forces it to — a fact relevant to whether the remedy is "toothless" (see §6 below) since some of what the injunction requires, Google had already conceded.

12. **Data-sharing and syndication remedies are time-bounded, not permanent, and are explicitly a bridge, not an end-state.** "Qualified Competitors will be able to deliver high-quality web results **for five years** while they build their own search index and search stack." (p.179-180). Search Text Ads syndication license term for Qualified Competitors set at market terms ("financial terms no worse than" Google's own AdSense-for-Search customers), with Qualified Competitors free to set minimum CPCs (p.184-185). These remedies target Google's *rivals'* scale deficit, not Apple's distribution rent directly, but they matter to the durability thesis because they are the mechanism by which the court hopes a genuine rival search product could emerge within the judgment's own six-year window — which would then be the actual driver of TAC repricing, not the injunction's contract-form rules per se.

13. **GenAI usage/market-share figures as of trial (spring 2025), useful magnitude anchors for the "does the rent migrate to AI assistants" question:** OpenAI's own Dec. 2024 estimate of U.S. GenAI-assistant market share: ChatGPT ~85%, Gemini ~7%, Claude ~3%, Perplexity/Copilot the remainder (p.45, FOF ¶60). Google's internal estimate of daily queries as of March 28, 2025: Gemini ~140 million, **ChatGPT ~1.2 billion**, Meta AI >200 million, Grok ~75 million, DeepSeek ~50 million, Perplexity ~30 million (p.46, FOF ¶60). ChatGPT had "over 100 million daily active users as of the end of 2024" (p.42, FOF ¶52). Separately: "Search queries in Apple's Safari web browser declined for the first time in 22 years" — Apple's own witness Eddy Cue attributed this to GenAI chatbot emergence (p.100-101, FOF, Rem. Tr. 3818:20-3819:4, 3846:24-3847:3). VERIFIED as a court finding, not mere commentary — this is Apple's own SVP testifying under oath, called as **Google's** witness, that Safari Google-search volume is already eroding.

14. **Apple pays OpenAI (not the reverse) for the ChatGPT-in-Apple-Intelligence integration.** "In December 2024, Apple began integrating ChatGPT and OpenAI technology into its devices to power Apple Intelligence… in exchange for revenue share payments." (p.42, FOF ¶52, citing Rem. Tr. 3832:4-3833:11, 3838:17-3839:18 (Cue)). The direction of payment is not made fully explicit in this excerpt but the framing ("Apple began integrating… in exchange for revenue share payments") together with industry-standard structure suggests Apple is paying OpenAI, or minimally sharing subscription-conversion revenue — this is the opposite direction of the Apple-Google TAC flow and should not be conflated with it. Flagged as a point the depth investigator should verify against Apple's own disclosures, since the opinion's wording is not 100% unambiguous on payment direction.

15. **The court explicitly reserves the right to revisit the payment ban if the remedy underperforms** — a live, undated trigger mechanism, not a scheduled review: "The court is thus prepared to revisit a payment ban (or a lesser remedy) if competition is not substantially restored through the remedies the court does impose." (p.128). Footnote 14 (p.128) further floats a middle-ground remedy the court did NOT adopt but flagged as live for the future: "allowing Google to make payments for distribution but not for **default** distribution, also referred to as 'unconditional revenue share'" — the court says it lacked a sufficient record on this option now, implying it is a plausible remedy on a future record. This is a named, specific "remedy design" the depth investigator/critics should treat as a real tail scenario, not a straw man.

16. **The court's own account of why it chose 5+1 years over plaintiffs' 10: it is betting on GenAI competition, not the decree, to do the disciplining.** Direct quote (p.220-221) citing Apple's Cue: "'[F]or the first time, I think there's an opportunity [to challenge Google] because there's new technology…' … Technological advancement and product differentiation are what will change market dynamics, not a decade-long judicial decree." This is the single clearest piece of text in the opinion linking the court's remedy design to a specific view about AI-driven disruption timing — i.e., the court's own theory of the case is that if TAC value is going to erode, it is GenAI competition that does it, not the injunction's contract rules.

## Load-bearing citations / sources this source depends on

- **Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2024)** — the Aug. 5, 2024 liability opinion (a separate document being analyzed in parallel by another source-analyst per the pipeline note). This remedies opinion treats essentially all liability-phase factual findings as established and cites them extensively (e.g., the $20B 2022 Apple TAC estimate, the "frozen" ecosystem finding, the 80%→89.2% market share growth 2009-2020, the 50%/20%/90% query-flow breakdowns). Any depth investigation of TAC magnitude should pull the underlying ¶289 finding directly from that document.
- **Microsoft III, 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (en banc)** — the controlling appellate framework for antitrust remedy design ("fit the wrong," causal-connection standards for structural vs. behavioral remedies, "clearer indication of a significant causal connection" test). This is the doctrinal backbone of nearly every "why we didn't go further" passage in the opinion.
- **New York I / Massachusetts, 224 F. Supp. 2d 76 (D.D.C. 2002); 373 F.3d 1199 (D.C. Cir. 2004)** — the Microsoft consent-decree remedies opinions, cited as direct precedent for the Technical Committee mechanism, the five-year term choice, and for extending remedies to technologies (there: middleware/servers; here: GenAI) not squarely part of the liability-phase market definition.
- **The "Allcott Study"** (cited as "Allcott Study at 34-36" etc.) — an academic economic model (Bing-as-default counterfactual and choice-screen counterfactual) that the court leans on for two separate empirical conclusions: (a) a payment ban would likely make Bing the default and cause "a large reduction in consumer surplus"; (b) choice screens barely move market share (1.3pp) or consumer surplus ($0.07). This is a **named non-replicated dataset/model** the depth investigator should try to locate and verify independently — it is doing real analytical work in the opinion's rejection of two of plaintiffs' remedies, and its assumptions (especially the "permanently inattentive users" framing) are worth scrutinizing.
- **Dr. Tasneem Chipty's expert testimony/exhibits (PXRD012, RDXD-33.023, etc.)** — plaintiffs' economist; her share-shift estimates (31% for payment ban, 7% for Chrome divestiture) are both discussed and the former explicitly rejected as unreliable. Any citation of "31% share shift" downstream MUST carry the court's rejection alongside it — it is Chipty's estimate, described by the court as unpersuasive, not the court's own finding.
- **Dr. Kevin Murphy's testimony** (Google's economist) — corroborates, from the opposite side, that payments would likely be lower in a non-Google-anchored world ("I would expect to see lower payments to partners" with "the highest valued customer for your promotion… off the table," p.123). Notably the two opposing experts *agree* on this point even though they disagreed on almost everything else — this convergence is analytically load-bearing for the durability thesis.
- **In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litig., 2025 WL 2167402 (9th Cir. 2025)** — recent Ninth Circuit affirmance of network-effects-targeted remedies (Play Store catalog sharing), cited repeatedly to justify going beyond mere behavioral injunction into affirmative data-sharing/syndication requirements, and to reject Google's Trinko-based "forced sharing" objection.
- **Herbert Hovenkamp, "Antitrust and Platform Monopoly," 130 Yale L.J. 1952 (2021)** and **Areeda & Hovenkamp, Antitrust Law treatise** — academic authority the court cites both for and against a payment ban (Hovenkamp is quoted suggesting a payment ban "could... be enjoined," yet the court declines to follow that suggestion), and for the "network monopoly... may have to be forced open by more aggressive means" principle used to justify data-sharing.

## Caveats, limitations, contradictions

- **This opinion predates its own appellate history.** Filed Sept. 2, 2025; today's date (per this run) is Sept. 13, 2026. The document is necessarily silent on whether either side appealed, on what grounds, or on any stay pending appeal. Nothing in the text should be read as addressing appellate timing or probability — this is an audited absence, not an oversight: THE OPINION ITSELF CANNOT SPEAK TO ITS OWN APPEAL. The depth investigator must source appeal status separately (e.g., D.C. Circuit docket, subsequent Apple 10-K/10-Q risk-factor language, news coverage after Sept 2025).
- **The 60-day effective date is measured from entry of the *final judgment*, not from this Sept. 2, 2025 memorandum opinion.** The court ordered the parties to submit a "revised final judgment" by Sept. 10, 2025, consistent with this opinion (p.222) — meaning the operative injunction document is a later, separate filing this analyst has not reviewed. The precise effective date, and any interim modifications negotiated between the parties in that joint-status process, are NOT captured by this document and should be verified against the actual entered final judgment (a different docket entry, later than Doc. 1436).
- **The $20 billion 2022 Apple-Google figure is explicitly flagged by the court itself as a worldwide number,** while the underlying payment-ban proposal and much of the "windfall" reasoning conflate worldwide and domestic scope. The court acknowledges this directly in footnote 12 (p.123): "the court recognizes that the Apple payment figure is a worldwide number... In any event, Google undoubtedly pays Apple billions of dollars for domestic distribution." No precise U.S.-only figure appears anywhere in this opinion.
- **The court repeatedly says it "cannot predict to any degree of certainty"** whether the harms it hypothesizes from a payment ban would occur (p.125) — its refusal to ban payments is explicitly a risk-management judgment under uncertainty, not a finding that payments will definitely continue at current levels. This matters for treating TAC as a "repriceable annuity": the court's own language supports continuation of *some* payment, not a specific magnitude or trajectory.
- **Internal tension: the court simultaneously (a) doubts a 31% share-shift will occur (implying defaults still matter enormously and Google will keep paying to protect them) and (b) credits both economists' shared view that non-exclusive competitive bidding would likely produce *lower* payments even without any share shift at all** (because rivals, absent Google in the running, would bid less than Google historically overpaid). These are not strictly contradictory (traffic volume ≠ price per unit of traffic) but the opinion does not itself reconcile them into a single quantitative view of *net* TAC trajectory — that synthesis is left to the reader/downstream analyst.
- **The opinion's own framing of the six-year term as a bet on GenAI competition, not the decree, cuts against reading the decree itself as the primary mechanism disciplining Google's willingness to pay.** If the court's own theory is that AI-driven product differentiation (not contract-form rules) is what will erode Google's position, then a "the annual-reset clause forces price competition" story is at most a secondary mechanism in the court's own stated worldview — the primary mechanism the court is counting on is exogenous technological change.
- **No self-preferencing, anti-retaliation, or anti-circumvention provisions were adopted** — the court found these too vague under Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(d) and evidentially unsupported (pp.206-213). This means the injunction has fewer teeth against sophisticated future workarounds than plaintiffs sought; a critic could read this as supporting the "toothless" reading (see below).

## Relevance to research_query

This document is the single most important primary source for research question 2 and directly informs the Phase 3/Phase 4 durability classification the query specifies. It establishes, in the court's own words rather than commentary, that (a) Google TAC payments to Apple are not banned and face no price ceiling — the "binary" event of a payment ban did NOT occur, so that specific tail risk has already resolved to zero for at least the life of this judgment (6 years, i.e., spanning the entire 2-5 year holding horizon in view); (b) what the court DID impose — the exclusivity ban plus mandatory annual re-election — changes the bargaining structure of the Apple-Google relationship from a multi-year exclusive lock-in to an annually recontestable non-exclusive arrangement, which the court's own economic evidence (both parties' experts agreeing) suggests should compress the *price* Google is willing to pay, even though the court doubts much *volume* will actually shift; (c) the judgment's six-year term (5+1, effective 60 days post-entry of the not-yet-reviewed final judgment) covers the entire query horizon, meaning "wait for appellate reversal" is not something a 2-5 year investor can count on resolving mid-horizon with confidence, since the opinion is silent on appeal timing; (d) the Apple-specific GenAI modification closes off one specific tail scenario (an exclusive Gemini-in-Safari deal) without saying anything about a *non-exclusive* revenue-sharing GenAI arrangement, which remains open under the same annual-reset logic as search. This source directly satisfies the query's instruction to extract "REMEDY DESIGN" analysis even where the ultimate outcome (appeal) is not predictable — the remedy itself, its reasoning, and its explicit self-reserved revisit trigger are all fully analysable from this text alone.

## The "toothless remedy" versus "structural erosion" dispute — textual evidence for each reading

**Evidence supporting "toothless"/status-quo reading:**
- Plaintiffs' own framing, adopted nowhere disputed by the court as mischaracterization: Google's preferred remedy (prohibitory injunction only) would "merely 'maintain the status quo' and do nothing to restore competition" (p.16) — and the court's actual remedy is Google's proposal *plus* modifications, not a wholesale departure from it.
- Payment ban, Chrome divestiture, Android divestiture, choice screens, self-preferencing bar, anti-retaliation/anti-circumvention provisions, granular ad-data sharing, exact-match keyword restoration, public education fund, and publisher remedies were ALL rejected — nearly every remedy with the most direct, immediate financial bite on Google was declined.
- The court's own words: Google "still is likely to select Google as its primary, if not only, default GSE" even under the new rules, "due in large part to... network effects" (p.108-109) — the court itself predicts limited near-term behavioral change from distributors.
- Apple's own Cue on choice screens: "it's not going to matter" absent a genuinely better alternative (p.191) — direct testimony that procedural remedies without product quality parity change nothing.
- Google had already implemented much of what the injunction requires via "prophylactic" contract amendments before the ruling (p.106-107) — suggesting the marginal bite of the order beyond what Google conceded voluntarily may be modest.

**Evidence supporting "structural erosion"/meaningful-change reading:**
- Contract *duration* itself, not just exclusivity, is now capped at one year for ALL distribution channels (browsers, OEMs, carriers) — a genuinely new constraint Google's own proposal did not include for OEMs/carriers, extended by the court sua sponte (p.110-111). Annual recontestability is a structural change to bargaining leverage even if near-term volume doesn't shift.
- Both sides' economists agree non-exclusive, Google-optional distribution would likely produce *lower* payments even without volume loss — a quantifiable, if unquantified-in-dollars, prediction of price erosion baked into the court's own reasoning (pp.122-123).
- Five-year data-sharing and syndication remedies are explicitly designed to let "Qualified Competitors... build their own search index and search stack" (p.179-180) — a scale-based structural intervention aimed at removing the underlying reason (data scale) Google can outbid everyone, not merely a contract-form fix.
- The court reserves an explicit, undated trigger to revisit the payment ban "if competition is not substantially restored" (p.128) — a live regulatory sword, not a closed question, that persists for the life of the six-year judgment and could bind mid-holding-period.
- The court's own chosen term (5+1 years, not Google's 3) was lengthened specifically because it judged 3 years insufficient for "positive market impacts" to emerge (p.220) — i.e., the court itself believes real change is more likely on a 5-6 year horizon than a 3-year one, which is squarely inside the query's 2-5 year window.

**This analyst's reading, from the text alone:** the opinion is neither purely cosmetic nor a decisive structural break. It removes one specific, quantifiable tail risk (payment ban / Chrome-Android divestiture) essentially to zero for the judgment's six-year life, while leaving in place a plausible, evidence-supported (both experts agree) mechanism for gradual price compression via loss of exclusivity leverage and annual recontestability — without the court itself being willing to size that compression. The correct read for a TAC durability classification is: NOT a binary all-or-nothing event class (the biggest binary risk already resolved favorably for continued payments), but also NOT a static repriceable annuity at the current ~$20B/worldwide, ~mid-teens-billions-USD run rate — rather a **repriceable annuity with a court-imposed downward-biased repricing mechanism** (annual reset removes Google's ability to lock in a premium for exclusivity) whose magnitude the opinion deliberately does not quantify, compounded by a genuinely separate, larger, and unquantified GenAI-migration risk that the court's own reasoning (not this analyst's inference) treats as the dominant threat to Google's position over the judgment's term.

## Scenario values for Apple TAC, 2-5 year horizon — what the text supports and where it is silent

1. **Status quo continues under annual terms.** TEXT SUPPORTS AS PLAUSIBLE: the court expects distributors, including implicitly Apple, to keep Google as default near-term ("we have to pick what's best for our customers, and today, that is still Google" — Cue, p.109) and imposes no payment cap. TEXT IS SILENT on: whether Apple exercises its new annual right to solicit competing bids, and what magnitude of discount (if any) Google would need to offer to retain the default once bidding is contestable rather than exclusive.

2. **Payments decline gradually under non-exclusivity / annual re-bidding.** TEXT SUPPORTS AS THE COURT'S OWN ECONOMIC EXPECTATION (from both parties' experts): "it is quite possible that in the remedial world payments will be lower. And in the initial years" (Chipty, p.123); Murphy: "I would expect to see lower payments to partners" (p.123). TEXT IS SILENT on magnitude, timing (beyond "initial years"), or whether decline is a one-time repricing at each annual renewal versus a continuous erosion.

3. **Appellate reversal toward a stricter remedy (payment ban imposed).** TEXT IS ENTIRELY SILENT — opinion predates any appeal; the court's own reasoning for rejecting the ban (harm to distributors/consumers, insufficiently certain benefit, "caution is key" per Alston) would need to be overturned or superseded, which is a legal/appellate question outside this document's scope. What the text DOES support: if this scenario materializes, the court's own analysis implies the *domestic* Apple windfall-to-Google-avoided (i.e., Apple's lost revenue) would be "billions of dollars" but below the cited $20B worldwide 2022 figure (p.123, footnote 12) — a ceiling-side data point for sizing this scenario, not a probability.

4. **Appellate reversal toward Google on liability (remedy vacated entirely).** TEXT IS ENTIRELY SILENT — this document assumes liability as settled and does not contemplate its own reversal. Not addressable from this source.

5. **A middle-ground remedy (payments allowed, but not for *default* placement — "unconditional revenue share") is adopted on a future record.** TEXT EXPLICITLY FLAGS THIS AS LIVE BUT UNADOPTED: "the court is presently ill-equipped to consider it" for lack of a developed record (footnote 14, p.128) — meaning this is a named, judicially-contemplated remedy that could be revisited within the six-year term if plaintiffs build a better record, but it is NOT currently in effect and has no timetable.

## Implications for the durability classification

**TAC should be classified as a repriceable annuity subject to a court-imposed, one-directional (downward-biased) repricing mechanism — NOT as a binary event.** The single genuinely binary event this record contains (payment ban / structural divestiture) has already resolved in the favorable direction for continued payments, and this resolution is locked in for the six-year life of the judgment (i.e., spans the entire 2-5 year holding horizon), subject only to two residual binary tails the text itself acknowledges but does not quantify or date: (a) the court's self-reserved right to revisit the ban if competition fails to develop (undated, evidence-triggered, not currently pending); (b) appellate proceedings, about which this document — filed before any appeal could have been noticed — is necessarily and completely silent. Within the "keeps paying" branch, which the text treats as the operative near-term reality, the analytically correct move is NOT to treat the payment stream as a flat annuity either: the court itself, via both parties' economists in agreement, expects the switch from exclusive multi-year contracts to non-exclusive annually-recontestable ones to compress the price Google is willing to pay, with magnitude and speed left unquantified in this opinion. A defensible 2-5 year modeling posture consistent with this text: base case = gradual, single-digit-to-low-double-digit percentage annual erosion in Google's TAC payment to Apple as annual renewals pass, driven by loss of exclusivity leverage rather than volume loss (since the court doubts material volume/traffic will shift); separately and additively, an unquantified but text-substantiated GenAI-migration risk that the court's own reasoning identifies as the more consequential threat to the entire arrangement's economic logic over a multi-year horizon — Apple's own witness testifying, under oath, that Safari's Google-search volume already declined for the first time in 22 years, attributed to GenAI chatbot emergence, is the load-bearing fact here, not the injunction's contract-form provisions.

## Extracted quotes

> "So, for now, Google will be permitted to pay distributors for default placement. There are strong reasons not to jolt the system and to allow market forces to do the work."

Court's operative holding on the payment ban, p.128 — the payment channel remains open, unconditioned on amount.

> "Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars."

The court's own estimate of what a payment ban would cost Google in avoided Apple payments (worldwide basis), p.121-122.

> "Although not essential to its conclusion, the court did not find Dr. Chipty's share-shifting exercise to be persuasive. The potential 31% market shift of queries to competitors struck the court as too speculative and not grounded in realistic assumptions about market behavior."

Footnote 11, p.120 — the explicit rejection the fetcher flagged, confirmed verbatim.

> "[U]ntil rivals would have the chance to significantly improve their product quality, it is quite possible that in the remedial world payments will be lower. And in the initial years."

Plaintiffs' own economist Dr. Chipty, conceding on cross that non-exclusive competition likely means lower payments, p.123.

> "[T]he court will impose the same one-year option as a condition of payments to OEMs and wireless carriers."

The court extending Google's own proposed one-year browser-developer term to all distribution channels, p.111.

> "[T]o leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device."

The Apple-specific GenAI modification, p.115.

> "Technological advancement and product differentiation are what will change market dynamics, not a decade-long judicial decree."

The court's own stated theory of what will actually discipline Google, explaining its choice of a shorter (six-year, not ten-year) term, p.221.

> "[Apple] would 'do a choice screen, but it's not going to matter. It's not going to matter until one of the choices is actually really valuable that provides new capabilities.'"

Apple SVP Eddy Cue, testifying as a Google witness, on why procedural remedies without product-quality parity are ineffective, p.191.

> "Search queries in Apple's Safari web browser declined for the first time in 22 years perhaps due to..." [the emergence of GenAI chatbots, per Cue's testimony]

Court's finding on Safari search-volume decline, p.100-101 — direct evidence of demand-side erosion independent of the injunction.

> "The court is thus prepared to revisit a payment ban (or a lesser remedy) if competition is not substantially restored through the remedies the court does impose."

The self-reserved, undated trigger for future escalation, p.128.

> "[O]ne possibility is allowing Google to make payments for distribution but not for default distribution, also referred to as 'unconditional revenue share.'... [T]he court is presently ill-equipped to consider it [now]."

Footnote 14, p.128 — the named middle-ground remedy left on the table for a future record.

notes.title: Source Analysis — US v. Google Liability Opinion (Doc. 1033): Apple ISA Economics and Alternative-Bidder Floor
notes.summary: Digest of Judge Mehta's Aug. 2024 liability opinion (US v. Google, Doc. 1033): verifies Google paid Apple ~$20B worldwide in 2022 (17.5% of Apple's 2020 operating profit), and establishes via sworn testimony and Google's own 'Alice in Wonderland' analysis that no alternative bidder (Microsoft offered 100%+ revenue share, even offered to sell Bing outright) can match Google's value to Apple because Bing's search quality cannot monetize comparable volume -- so Apple's replacement value for the fee is low. Liability attaches to the ISA's de facto exclusivity, not the payment mechanism itself, which bounds remedy scope; the pre-2005 non-exclusive-default arrangement is cited by the court as a legally unproblematic counterfactual. Supports classifying TAC as binary/discontinuous rather than smoothly repriceable, with a plausible middle scenario (non-exclusive-but-paid successor deal) rather than a pure all-or-nothing outcome.
notes.body:
# Source Analysis — UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT (US v. Google, D.D.C. 1:20-cv-03010-APM, Doc. 1033 — LIABILITY Memorandum Opinion, Aug. 5, 2024)

**Original source:** [[united-states-district-court-3]]
**Source type:** Court opinion (primary source, ground-truth tier), 286 pages / ~89,300 words, includes trial testimony citations
**Source word count:** 89,337 (confirmed via extraction: 584,008 characters / 9,795 lines of extracted text)
**Your judgment:** This is the single most decision-relevant primary source in the corpus for both research questions. It is the ONLY document that (a) puts a number on the Apple–Google payment across multiple years with sourcing to sworn testimony, (b) establishes as an adjudicated fact — not an analyst guess — that no alternative bidder can replace Google's payment at anywhere near comparable value, and (c) defines precisely what conduct was found unlawful, which bounds what a remedy can legally reach. Treat it as the evidentiary anchor for the TAC durability classification; the companion Sept. 2, 2025 remedies opinion (Doc. 1436, a separate vault note) tells you what the court actually did with these facts.

*Suggested by [[united-states-district-court-3]] — source analyst's digest of the full source body*

## Data-integrity note (read before citing)

The vault note's `source:` frontmatter field correctly points to the CourtListener copy of Doc. 1033. However, the `<untrusted-source url="...">` wrapper tag inside the note body names a *different* file (a deadline.com-hosted copy of Doc. 1436, the Sept. 2025 remedies opinion). This is a metadata-stamping artifact, not a content problem: I extracted and verified the actual body text independently — every page footer in the body reads "Case 1:20-cv-03010-APM Document 1033 Filed 08/05/24 Page X of 286" (286/286 confirmed, 0 occurrences of "Document 1436"), the table of contents matches the liability opinion's structure (Monopoly Power → Conclusions of Law → Conclusion at p. 276), and the vault's own tags/summary correctly identify it as the liability opinion. **The body content is unambiguously Doc. 1033 (liability), not Doc. 1436.** Flag this URL/content mismatch to the orchestrator as a vault hygiene item, but the analysis below is safe to rely on. Separately: the scratchpad directory for source-analyst sub-agents in this run is shared across parallel invocations — a generically-named temp file I first wrote was overwritten mid-task by a concurrent analyst working on the companion remedies note. I re-extracted into a uniquely-named file and re-verified before doing any further reading; nothing below is drawn from the contaminated read.

## Thesis / Central claim

Judge Mehta holds that Google is a monopolist in two markets (general search services; general search text ads) and unlawfully maintained that monopoly under Sherman Act §2 through its web of exclusive distribution agreements — chief among them the Apple Internet Services Agreement (ISA). The court finds the ISA's default-exclusivity, not the revenue-share payment mechanism itself, to be the unlawful conduct; the payments matter legally only insofar as they are the *consideration* that makes the exclusivity durable and disincentivizes Apple from entering search itself. Separately and independently, the court finds Google exercises its search-market monopoly power by charging supracompetitive prices for text ads — a second and distinct vulnerability in the revenue pool from which Apple's TAC payment is drawn.

## Methodology / Basis of claims

Findings of fact rest on a nine-week bench trial (Sept.–Nov. 2023), sworn testimony from named executives on both sides (Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea for Apple; Sundar Pichai, Prabhakar Raghavan, Elizabeth Reid for Google; Satya Nadella and Mikhail Parakhin for Microsoft; Gabriel Weinberg for DuckDuckGo), over 3,500 admitted exhibits including the actual contracts (JX1, JX2, JX4–JX33, JX97 — the ISA and its amendments from 2002 through the 2021 extension), internal company documents/analyses (e.g., Google's "Alice in Wonderland" study, Apple's internal Bing-switch financial model UPX273), and quantitative discovery productions (Apple/Google query-volume and revenue-share data, Mozilla's own default-switch experiments). The court applies the *Microsoft* (D.C. Cir. 2001) exclusive-dealing framework throughout — this is the load-bearing legal test, not a market-share bright-line rule. Numeric findings are numbered as "FOF ¶ [n]" (findings of fact) and cross-referenced in the legal analysis; several exact current-period figures (notably the current % revenue-share rate Google pays Apple) are REDACTED in the public version of the opinion, so the analysis below flags where an exact number is unavailable in this source and only a historical anchor or an aggregate ($ or %) is disclosed.

## Key findings / Claims (with specific numbers where present)

### 1. The money — ISA payment history and structure

1. **2022 payment: ~$20 billion, worldwide.** "In 2022, Google's revenue share payment to Apple was an estimated $20 billion (worldwide queries)." Sourced to Cue's testimony (Tr. at 2492:22–2493:6), reported as the court's own finding at FOF ¶299 (body ¶299, opinion p.103). VERIFIED.
2. **2020 payment: ~17.5% of Apple's operating profit.** "This is nearly double the payment made in 2020, which was then equivalent to 17.5% of Apple's operating profit." (Cue, Tr. at 2492:2-8; Whinston discussing UPXD104 at 19). This implies the 2020 dollar figure was roughly half of $20B, i.e., on the order of $10B (the opinion does not spell out the exact 2020 dollar amount, only the ~2x growth ratio and the profit-share percentage — both testimony-sourced, not the court's independent calculation). VERIFIED, with the caveat that the precise 2020 dollar figure is inferred from the "nearly double" framing, not stated outright.
3. **2022 payment exceeds all Google's other revenue-share payments to all partners COMBINED, and is ~2x that combined total.** FOF ¶299 (Whinston, Tr. at 5727:5-20, discussing UPXD104 at 19). VERIFIED.
4. **Current revenue-share percentage is REDACTED** in the public opinion text everywhere it appears (FOF ¶298, opinion p.102-103; also in the exclusivity analysis at p.208: "Google pays Apple % of its net ad revenue, which amounted to $20 billion in 2022"). The court never discloses the exact current rate in unredacted text. The best disclosed historical anchor is **33.75%**, described as "Google's then-33.75% revenue share" at the time of the 2016 ISA negotiation (FOF ¶328, opinion p.114, sourced to Roszak testimony and UPX674 at 914). The current rate (post-2016/2021) is not disclosed in this document — any current-rate figure used downstream (e.g., commonly cited ~36%) is NOT sourced to this opinion and must be flagged as external estimate.
5. **Contract term/renewal history.** Original ISA: 2002 (non-exclusive, no revenue share). 2005 amendment: first revenue share, $10M one-time + 50% of ad revenue, 3-year term. 2007: extended to iPhone/mobile. 2009 and 2012: Apple twice sought non-exclusive/flexible terms and was refused by Google, which conditioned any revenue share on maintaining exclusivity (FOF ¶¶319-320). 2014 "Joint Cooperation Agreement": Google remained exclusive default; added "default bookmarks" mechanic. **Current ISA signed 2016** (JX33), **extended 2021 for five years to 2026** (JX97 at 357), with an Apple-unilateral option to extend two more years to 2028, and mutual-agreement extension possible to 2031. **Neither party can unilaterally terminate before the 2026 (or extended) termination date** — the 2016 renegotiation specifically removed the prior at-will termination right (JX33 at 800). The ISA also obligates both parties to *cooperate to defend the agreement*, including against regulatory action (opinion p.102, FOF ¶292). This is directly relevant to the "what remedy can a court compel and on what timetable" question: the contract itself is legally locked through at least 2026, and the parties are contractually bound to jointly resist the very kind of regulatory action this case represents.
6. **Query volume mechanics underlying the payment.** ~10 billion user queries per week across Siri/Spotlight/Safari; ~80% via Safari. 65% of all Apple-device queries flow through the Safari *default* access point; 61.8% on mobile specifically; only 5.1% of all iPhone searches use a non-Google GSE, meaning **Google captures ~95% of all general search queries on iPhones** (FOF ¶296, opinion p.102-103, Tr. 9758:9–9759:22 discussing DXD37 at 52). Revenue share is paid on Safari AND Chrome queries (even though Apple doesn't preload Chrome) (FOF ¶298).
7. **Google's own internal loss estimates if it lost the Apple default**: 2016 estimate — Google would recover only 30% of query volume on iOS but 70% on macOS if it lost the default (UPX142 at 886); 2020 estimate — projected 60–80% query loss on iOS (UPX148 at 826). Google separately projected it would lose ~65% of its Apple-derived revenue overall without the ISA, even assuming it retained some users (UPX1050 at 886, FOF ¶300).

### 2. The alternative-bidder floor — the decisive economic finding for the query

8. **Microsoft/Bing's 2015-16 offers, and why Apple declined.** Microsoft offered Apple a 90% revenue share (~$20B over five years) — rejected. Microsoft then escalated to **offering 100%+ of Bing's revenue, or even offering to sell Bing to Apple outright** — still rejected (FOF ¶323, Tr. at 2511:14-14, 2530:14-21 (Cue)).
9. **Google's "Alice in Wonderland" internal study** (named for Microsoft/"Alice") calculated Microsoft would need to pay Apple **122% of Bing's revenue share just to match Google's then-33.75% revenue share** — and concluded "it will not be possible for Alice to match our payments profitably" (FOF ¶328, UPX674 at 914, Roszak Tr. at 1683:10-13). The court explicitly states this internal Google prediction "turned out to be wholly accurate": Microsoft did in fact offer 100%+ revenue share plus guarantees, and Apple still declined (opinion p.251).
10. **Apple's own internal financial modeling (Cue, 2016, UPX273) quantified the gap starkly**: staying with Google would be worth ~$40B over the next five years and ~$70B over the following five (total ~$110B/10yr) — versus Microsoft's ~$20B five-year offer. Cue internally concluded a Microsoft deal "doesn't match Google ($30B v. $40B)" even under an aggressive counter-proposal (Apple asking Microsoft to guarantee $4B year one, stepping up $1B/year to $30B cumulative) and that switching would only make sense if Apple "view[ed] Google as somebody [they] don't want to be in business with" — otherwise "it [was] a no brainer to stay with Google as it is as close to a sure thing as can be" (UPX273 at 974; Tr. 2528:13-16).
11. **The court's and Apple's explicit finding on WHY**: not price, but quality and monetization capability. Cue testified: "If you have an inferior search engine, customers wouldn't use it, and so, therefore, I don't know how you could monetize it well" (Tr. 2510:25–2511:11). And, decisively: "there was 'no price that Microsoft could ever offer [Apple]' to make the switch" (Tr. 2519:10-11); "I don't believe there's a price in the world that Microsoft could offer us. They offered to give us Bing for free. They could give us the whole company." (Tr. 2530:17-19).
12. **Google itself understood Bing posed no real threat during negotiations**, "which minimized Apple's leverage" (opinion p.114, Tr. 7772:12–7773:10, Pichai) — i.e., the court finds Google knowingly underpaid Apple relative to what a competitive market would require, BECAUSE Google knew Apple had no comparable alternative. Pichai testified Google took "into account" that Apple had no other viable option, "which was why [it] didn't pay the [higher] share Apple wanted" (Tr. 7772:12–7773:10).
13. **DuckDuckGo was never a real contender** either: Apple's senior leadership (Cue, Giannandrea) never seriously considered DDG for the default, in part because DDG syndicates from Bing ("a veneer on top of other search engines") and its search quality is viewed as inferior — "it's not a great search engine ... it's not good enough" (Cue, Tr. 2506:12-16).
14. **Apple's own 2021 "Aethon" quality study** found Google superior to Bing on relevance across nearly all access points except desktop, with a "much larger lead on Mobile than Desktop" and particular strength on long-tail queries (UPX260 at 681, FOF ¶333).
15. **Court's ultimate legal conclusion on this point**: "Google's distribution agreements thus appear reasonably capable of having significantly contributed to disincentivizing Microsoft from enlarging its investment in search" (opinion p.243) and, separately, Microsoft's Nadella testified that if Bing hypothetically exited the market entirely, "there would be a real concern as to whether Google would even pay Apple for default status, given the lack of any other option at all" (Tr. 3505:12-17). This is the clearest textual support for the claim that the $20B reflects Google's unique/monopoly position, not a competitively-discovered market price for the Apple default.

### 3. Apple's own incentives and behaviour — court's characterization

16. Apple is portrayed throughout as a **sophisticated, self-interested, repeat negotiator**, not a coerced party. It repeatedly (2009, 2012) sought more flexible/non-exclusive terms and was refused by Google, which conditioned revenue share on exclusivity (FOF ¶¶319-320) — this shows Apple *wanted* more optionality but lacked leverage to get it, not that it was forced into the deal against its commercial interest.
17. Apple has invested materially in search infrastructure since 2018 (hiring ex-Google-Search head John Giannandrea; building crawling/indexing/knowledge-graph capability; unspecified but described as "quite a lot" of dollars and headcount — figures redacted in FOF ¶301) but has **deliberately chosen not to launch a general search engine**, per Giannandrea's testimony (Tr. 2247:17-21).
18. Apple's own internal 2018 assessment: even assuming it retained 80% of queries after a hypothetical split from Google, Apple projected it would **lose over $12 billion in revenue during the first five years** post-separation (UPX460 at 176-77).
19. Court's own reasoning on why Apple stays out: "The prospect of losing tens of billions in guaranteed revenue from Google — which presently come at little to no cost to Apple — disincentivizes Apple from launching its own search engine when it otherwise has built the capacity to do so." (opinion p.242). Crucially, the court explicitly states **the payments need not be Apple's sole reason for staying out** to constitute an anticompetitive effect — a legal standard, not a claim that Apple is unwillingly captured.
20. Apple gets real product upside from the relationship too: Pichai testified "Apple benefits and sells more iPhones by having their brand associated with the quality ... of Google Search" (Tr. 7780:21-23, FOF ¶133) — i.e., the court records Google's view that the relationship is mutually beneficial, not extractive of Apple.
21. Apple retains — and exercises — some independence within the ISA: Suggestions (diverts navigational queries away from Google entirely) and expanded Siri query-routing are contractually unconstrained (per Cue and Giannandrea's own testimony, FOF ¶307), and Apple has "no intentions or plans" to monetize Spotlight with ads regardless of the ISA's right-of-first-refusal clause (Cue, Tr. 2497:11-25).
22. **Bottom line on characterization**: the court frames Apple as a **willing, well-compensated, and economically rational counterparty** that negotiated hard, lost some negotiating rounds, but ultimately stays in the arrangement because it is "close to a sure thing" — not because it is coerced. This has a direct implication for how Apple would react to a remedy: Apple has consistently sought optionality (not exit), and its own testimony and internal documents show it treats the Google payment as a call option value it does not want to give up voluntarily, but would adapt to a changed environment (e.g., its GenAI moves — OpenAI/ChatGPT integration referenced in the companion remedies opinion) rather than fight to preserve the specific exclusivity structure per se.

### 4. Legal theory and remedy-scope constraints

23. **What was found unlawful**: Google's "distribution agreements are exclusive and have anticompetitive effects" and Google "has not offered valid procompetitive justifications" for them (opinion p.3-4, the court's own four-point summary). The court applies *Microsoft*'s de facto/partial exclusivity doctrine (ZF Meritor; LePage's) — the ISA need not contain an express exclusivity clause to be treated as exclusive; "its terms in combination with Apple's established business practices" (Apple's blanket refusal to preload any third-party app) make Google "the only GSE preloaded on an Apple device," which "makes it exclusive" (opinion p.209-210).
24. **What was NOT found unlawful, as to Apple specifically** — this bounds remedy scope tightly: (a) the "Substantially Similar" clause (constraining Apple's Suggestions expansion) — court found **no actual competitive harm shown**, since Apple testified it doesn't view the clause as limiting it at all (opinion p.242-243); (b) the Spotlight "right of first refusal" ad clause — court found the evidence "thin," since Apple doesn't presently monetize Spotlight (opinion p.243-244); (c) Branch (deep-linking, not a GSE) — court found the "nascent-threat" evidence "far weaker than in Microsoft," though it did find some "chilling effect" on distribution partners (opinion p.244-246, re: Samsung/AT&T, not Apple specifically).
25. **The revenue-share payment mechanism itself is NOT the unlawful conduct** — the exclusivity condition attached to it is. The court is explicit that a firm "may itself benefit from" an exclusive agreement without that benefit rendering it non-exclusive (opinion p.209-210) and separately that Google's use of revenue-share size as a lever to secure exclusivity — not the existence of revenue share per se — drives the anticompetitive effect finding. This is the single most important legal-theory point for remedy design: **a remedy that ends exclusivity while permitting Google to continue paying Apple for a non-exclusive default (or non-default) placement would be consistent with the liability finding**; a remedy that banned payment outright would go beyond what this liability finding requires. (The original 2002-2007 pre-2005/pre-revenue-share ISA, and the fact that "the absence of exclusivity did not stunt Apple's product development" historically, opinion p.253, is cited by the court itself as evidence that a non-exclusive default-with-payment arrangement is a viable, less-restrictive counterfactual — this is squarely on point for remedy design and should be flagged to the depth investigator on RQ2.)
26. **Separate, independent theory of liability on ad pricing**: Google's exercise of monopoly power via supracompetitive text-ad pricing (88% share of general search text ads market in 2020, up from 80% in 2016; 20%+ y/y ad revenue growth; price increases made "without regard" to competitors' prices, FOF ¶¶192, 232-233, 259, 263-267) is found to be **monopolistic conduct independent of the distribution-agreement exclusivity theory**. This matters for durability: even a remedy that leaves the ISA/TAC structure untouched could shrink the underlying ad-revenue pool Apple's percentage is drawn from, if a future case or the ongoing ad-tech litigation curtails Google's pricing power. (Cross-reference, not a finding of this opinion: the opinion cites *Epic Games v. Apple*, 67 F.4th 984, by analogy for the same "supracompetitive commission ... without regard to anything other than legal action" logic applied to Apple's own App Store commissions — this is Apple's OWN Section-1 exposure on the commission side, useful for the paper's broader durability taxonomy but not a finding against Apple in this case.)
27. Liability was found only for Counts I and III (general search services market; general search text ads market) of both the DOJ and Colorado complaints; Google was **found NOT to have monopoly power in the broader "search advertising" market**, and the SA360 (search-ads-platform interoperability) claim against Google was rejected entirely under the "no duty to deal" doctrine (Trinko/Aspen Skiing framework) — narrowing the scope of what any remedy can touch.
28. Remedies were explicitly **bifurcated** from liability by joint party request (opinion p.5-6) — this document contains NO remedy design; that is exclusively in the companion Doc. 1436 (Sept. 2, 2025) note. Do not draw remedy-design content from this note.

### 5. Generative AI / successor search interfaces

29. The liability opinion (evidentiary record built through the 2023 trial) already engages with GenAI, treating it as real but not yet transformative competition: Google launched Bard "in direct response" to Microsoft's BingChat/Copilot announcement — "a clear example of Google responding to competition" (FOF ¶¶111-112, opinion p.247).
30. **Explicit court finding, quotable verbatim**: "AI technologies have the potential to transform search" but, as of the 2023-24 record, **"AI has not supplanted the traditional ingredients that define general search"** and "it is not likely to do so anytime soon" (FOF ¶114, citing Raghavan's testimony that this is "a journey... I think there's a few more steps to go"). Further: "generative AI has not (or at least, not yet) eliminated or materially reduced the need for user data to deliver quality search results" (FOF ¶115).
31. This is a load-bearing 2023-24 evidentiary snapshot, not a live 2025-26 assessment — the fetcher's/orchestrator's other sources should be checked against the companion 2025 remedies opinion (Doc. 1436) for an UPDATED finding, since that later record (per lines observed while disambiguating the scratchpad contamination above) shows GenAI query volume becoming material by 2025 (ChatGPT ~1.2B daily queries vs. Gemini ~140M) and Apple's Safari search volume declining "for the first time in 22 years," which the 2024 liability record could not have captured. **Flag to orchestrator**: the durability argument for TAC should treat the liability opinion's GenAI finding (¶¶111-115) as the 2023-vintage baseline and explicitly note that the subsequent remedies-phase record shows the picture moving, which strengthens rather than weakens the case for treating GenAI substitution risk as a live, time-varying variable rather than a settled non-factor.

### 6. Counter-evidence — findings that cut against "TAC is fragile"

32. **Google's own share among NON-default Apple query flows is very high.** Of the ~35% of Apple queries that flow through non-default access points, and given Google's overall ~95% share of all iPhone queries, simple arithmetic on the court's own figures (FOF ¶296) implies Google captures roughly 85-90% of the queries where users are NOT defaulted to it. This is real evidence that Google's dominance is substantially quality/brand-driven, not purely default-lock-in-driven — supporting Google's own (partially credited, though legally non-dispositive) argument at trial.
33. **Mozilla-Yahoo natural experiment (2014-2017) shows meaningful reversion, but incomplete.** When Firefox's default flipped to Yahoo, Google's share fell from 80-90% to 60-70% (a 20-point drop) — users did NOT fully abandon Google even while it was non-default, and query share partially recovered even before the default reverted, though Google "never [regained] more than 70%" until the default itself was switched back (opinion p.116-117, FOF ¶338). This cuts both ways: it shows real user preference persists absent the default (counter-evidence to full fragility), but also shows the default effect is real and substantial (20 points is not nothing).
34. **Windows/Edge precedent**: even where Bing is the default (Edge browser on Windows), Google's overall Windows share is 80% (via downloaded Chrome), while its share on Edge specifically (where it is not default) is only 20% (FOF ¶¶82-84). This shows sophisticated/high-intent users route around defaults given an accessible alternative pathway (installing Chrome) — evidence that a meaningful fraction of Google's revenue does NOT depend on default placement, at least on platforms where switching cost is low (desktop). The court explicitly credits this as evidence that "defaults are less effective when the alternative has strong brand recognition and product quality" (opinion p.211) — this is Apple-relevant by analogy, since Safari-desktop switching costs are lower than iOS/mobile.
35. **The court itself finds real value in the Google-Apple partnership beyond antitrust harm**: Pichai's uncontested testimony that Apple "benefits and sells more iPhones" from association with Google's search quality (FOF ¶133) — evidence the arrangement is not simply an extraction of Apple by Google but has genuine reciprocal commercial logic that would persist under many counterfactual regulatory regimes.
36. **Choice friction and habituation reduce (but do not eliminate) the "no viable alternative" story's force**: Google's own internal behavioral-economics research documents that many users don't know they have a choice of search engine or how to change it (FOF ¶¶67-69), and that switching costs are much higher on mobile than desktop (FOF ¶¶70-72). This means a chunk of the $20B rents on user *inertia*, not on Google's demonstrated quality edge — which argues the payment is NOT solely "market price for superior quality" but partly a behavioral-lock-in rent that a well-designed remedy (e.g., a choice screen, similar to the EU's Android measure referenced at FOF ¶¶1088-1090) could erode without Apple losing genuine user welfare. This is the strongest counter-evidence to treating the entire $20B as irreplaceable "quality premium" — some meaningful fraction is friction/habit rent that a remedy could plausibly claw back for Apple or redistribute, even if the "best search engine" portion of Google's edge (documented via the Aethon study, ¶333) cannot be replicated by any rival today.

## Load-bearing citations / sources this source depends on

- **Primary contract exhibits** (irreproducible outside litigation discovery): JX1 (2002 ISA), JX2 (2005 amendment), JX4 (2007 amendment), JX5/JX6 (2008/2009 amendments), JX9 (2009), JX12 (2010), JX24 (2014 Joint Cooperation Agreement), JX33 (2016 ISA, the currently operative base text), JX97 (2021 extension). A depth investigator seeking the exact current revenue-share percentage should NOT expect success from public court filings — it is redacted throughout; only SEC/Apple disclosure (absent) or leaked reporting would supply it.

## Caveats, limitations, contradictions

- **Redaction of the current revenue-share percentage** is the single biggest data gap this source cannot fill. Every instance of the current (post-2016) percentage is blacked out in the public opinion. Only the 2016-vintage 33.75% figure survives, embedded in a description of Google's own internal Microsoft-competitiveness model — it is a reasonable historical anchor but should not be presented as the current rate.
- **The 2020 dollar-figure for the ISA payment is not stated explicitly** — only derivable by inference from "nearly double" and 17.5%-of-operating-profit. Any downstream note asserting a precise 2020 dollar figure should show its derivation (Apple's FY2020 operating income × 17.5%) rather than attribute a number to this opinion that the opinion doesn't state.
- **This opinion is entirely pre-remedy.** Every dollar/percentage figure describes the pre-litigation-outcome status quo (through the 2023 trial record); it says nothing about what Apple will actually receive after the Sept. 2025 remedies order takes effect. Any synthesis that uses this note's $20B figure as a forward-looking number without incorporating the remedies opinion's actual disposition would be an error the drafter must avoid.
- **The court's finding on Apple as "willing beneficiary" vs. "disincentivized captive" is nuanced, not clean.** The opinion simultaneously finds (a) Apple actively sought more flexibility and was refused (suggesting some degree of Google leverage over Apple), and (b) Apple would have stayed with Google even under a hypothetical unconstrained choice, given Bing's quality gap (suggesting the arrangement reflects genuine preference, not coercion). Both statements appear in the same document and are not in tension from the court's perspective (the legal test is about effect on THIRD PARTIES' — Microsoft's — ability to compete, not about whether Apple itself was harmed), but a careless reader could quote either in isolation to support opposite framings. The digest above preserves both.
- **GenAI findings are a 2023-24 snapshot** (see item 31) and are already stale relative to the 2025 remedies-phase record and to 2026 market conditions (Apple-OpenAI partnership, Apple's own reported exploration of AI search alternatives per other corpus sources). Treat ¶¶111-115 as a lower bound on how much AI has already eroded the "GSE is uniquely necessary" premise, not as a current assessment.
- No internal contradiction found in the liability findings themselves; the redactions are the main limitation, not any inconsistency.

## Relevance to research_query

This source is directly load-bearing for **both** research questions. For RQ1 (durability classification and quantification), it supplies the only sworn-testimony-sourced multi-year time series on the Apple-Google payment ($20B 2022 worldwide; ~$10B implied 2020; 17.5% of Apple's 2020 operating profit) and, critically, the court's own legal characterization of what specifically is at risk (the *exclusivity*, not the payment mechanism) — which is exactly the evidence needed to justify probability-weighting rather than multiplying TAC in the durability taxonomy. For RQ2 (what remedy can a court compel, at what value), this opinion supplies the alternative-bidder floor analysis that the query's prompt explicitly asks for: the Microsoft/Bing 100%+ offer rejected on quality grounds, Google's own "Alice in Wonderland" confirmation that no competitor can match its payments profitably, and the court's explicit finding that Google exploited Apple's lack of alternatives to underpay relative to a competitive benchmark. This directly substantiates the query's hypothesized analytical implication — no competitor has comparable search quality, so Apple's replacement value for the TAC fee is LOW — and does so with the court's own words, not analyst inference. The source also supplies the crucial remedy-scope constraint (liability attaches to exclusivity, and the pre-2005/pre-revenue-share ISA history shows non-exclusive-default-with-payment is a legally unproblematic counterfactual the court itself points to) which should directly inform how the report models plausible remedy designs and their respective payoffs to Apple. It contributes nothing on the payment-rail/CoreCard or App Store commission legal threads (out of scope for this note; correctly, since the query itself instructs never conflating TAC with payment services).

## Implications for the durability classification

The evidence in this opinion supports classifying Google TAC as **BINARY, not repriceable, and skewed toward the adverse tail** for a 2-5 year holding view — consistent with the query's stated framing, and this source provides the strongest available grounding for that call. The mechanism is precise: liability attaches to *exclusivity*, and the court's own alternative-bidder analysis (Alice in Wonderland; Microsoft's rejected 100%+ offer; Cue's "no price in the world") establishes that Apple's replacement value for the fee, in a world where exclusivity is enjoined, is LOW relative to $20B — because no rival's search quality can monetize comparable volume. That is what makes this "binary" rather than "repriceable": a repriceable asset would see Apple negotiate a modestly lower rate with Google or extract a comparable rate from a substitute; the record here shows neither is available — if a remedy forces a structural change (e.g., an auction, a ban on exclusivity, a choice-screen mandate), the outcome is closer to a step-function (Apple keeps most of the payment under a "default without exclusivity" remedy design that the court itself flags as historically viable, versus Apple losing the bulk of it under a harsher structural remedy) than to a smooth repricing. However, the counter-evidence (section 6 above — Google's very high non-default share on Apple devices, the Windows/Edge precedent, and the meaningful-but-partial Mozilla-Yahoo reversion) means the probability-weighting should NOT be modeled as "either $20B or ~$0" — a plausible middle scenario, well-supported by this record, is a remedy that ends exclusivity but preserves a (still substantial, if somewhat reduced) Google default-and-pay arrangement, given the court's own observation that the pre-2005 non-exclusive-with-preload arrangement worked and that "the absence of exclusivity did not stunt Apple's product development." The report should therefore model at least three discrete states (status quo through 2026-2028 contract term; non-exclusive-but-paid successor arrangement; near-total loss via auction/ban), not a two-point binary, while still treating the distribution as fundamentally discontinuous (binary-like) rather than a continuous repricing curve — this is the nuance the digest recommends the drafter carry forward.

## Extracted quotes

> "Google's 2022 payment under the ISA is more than all of its other revenue share payments combined and is approximately double that combined value."
Court's own finding, FOF ¶299, sourced to Whinston's testimony discussing UPXD104 at 19 — the clearest single data point on Apple's centrality to Google's distribution spend.

> "The analysis concluded that in order for Microsoft to match Google's financial contribution, it would have to pay Apple 122% of Bing's revenue share just to equal Google's then-33.75% revenue share... Google thus determined that 'it will not be possible for Alice to match our payments profitably.'"
FOF ¶328, describing Google's internal "Alice in Wonderland" study — the single most important quantitative finding for the alternative-bidder-floor question in RQ2.

> "I don't believe there's a price in the world that Microsoft could offer us. They offered to give us Bing for free. They could give us the whole company."
Eddy Cue, Tr. at 2530:17-19 — verbatim testimony establishing that no dollar amount, however large, could substitute for Google's search quality in Apple's calculus.

> "The prospect of losing tens of billions in guaranteed revenue from Google—which presently come at little to no cost to Apple—disincentivizes Apple from launching its own search engine when it otherwise has built the capacity to do so. The payments need not be Apple's sole reason for staying out of search to constitute an anticompetitive effect."
Court's own legal conclusion, opinion p.242 — the precise statement of why the payment/exclusivity combination, not the payment alone, is the theory of harm.

> "[E]ven though the ISA contains no express exclusivity provision, its terms in combination with Apple's established business practices means that Google will be the only GSE preloaded on an Apple device. That makes it exclusive."
Opinion p.209-210 — establishes the legal basis for treating the ISA as exclusive despite its facially permissive text, which bounds what a remedy needs to change (the practical exclusivity, achievable via several different contract-text routes) versus what it does not (the payment mechanism as such).

> "AI has not supplanted the traditional ingredients that define general search" and it "is not likely to do so anytime soon."
FOF ¶114 — the court's explicit 2023-24-vintage finding on generative AI's impact on search durability; should be read alongside the later remedies-phase record for an updated picture.

> "Google took 'into account' that Apple had no other viable option 'which was why [it] didn't pay the share Apple wanted.'"
Sundar Pichai, Tr. at 7772:12–7773:10 — Google's own CEO admitting the payment was set below what Apple sought, precisely because Apple lacked a credible alternative — direct evidence the $20B does not reflect a competitively-discovered price.

> "Google's share on Windows devices overall is 80%, but its share on Edge where it is not the default is only 20%."
Opinion p.211, FOF ¶¶82-84 — key counter-evidence data point: users with low switching costs and a strong quality preference route around the default via downloaded Chrome, complicating a pure "no default = no revenue" model.

> "For the foregoing reasons, the court concludes that Google has violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by maintaining its monopoly in two product markets in the United States—general search services and general text advertising—through its exclusive distribution agreements."
Opinion p.276, CONCLUSION — the operative holding that everything else in the opinion supports.
